query: For reported HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, what testable hypothesis could enable Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior to be predicted more rapidly and accurately under tensile and fracture testing than with established simulations? State the hypothesized rationale, the measurable gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency, circumstances in which the hypothesis may fail, relevant supporting evidence, and a predeclared result from independent measurements that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A machine learning surrogate model built on key microstructural descriptors of the hierarchical heterostructure in as‐cast HfNbTiVAl10 can predict its Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior under tensile and fracture testing more rapidly (approximately one order of magnitude faster) and with prediction errors within 15–20% compared to established DFT/atomistic simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfNbTiVAl10 exhibiting a hierarchical heterostructure characterized by a mixture of phase regions (e.g., secondary precipitates or heterogeneously distributed matrix phases) and associated lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Develop and validate a machine learning model that uses experimentally measured microstructural descriptors (e.g., phase fractions, misfit volumes, and lattice distortion parameters) as input features to predict the key mechanical properties.
generation.conditions: Tensile tests and fracture testing performed at room temperature with controlled strain rates (~10^(-3) s^(-1)) and ambient atmosphere, with concurrent microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM) for descriptor validation.
generation.structural_mediator: The hierarchical microstructure—including heterogeneously distributed phases and coherent interfaces that mediate dislocation motion and strain localization—acts as the structural mediator affecting elastic and plastic responses.
generation.mechanism: The surrogate model leverages the correlation between microstructural parameters (such as phase distribution, lattice misfit, and precipitate characteristics) and mechanical responses to capture the underlying deformation mechanisms (solid-solution and precipitation strengthening, load transfer at interfaces) that govern Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will deliver rapid predictions (roughly 10× faster than traditional simulations) with accuracy improvements such that the predicted values match experimental tensile and fracture properties within a 15–20% error margin compared to baseline DFT-based or atomistic simulation methods.
generation.baseline: Conventional simulations (DFT and atomistic models) that require extensive computational resources and time to simulate elastic and fracture responses of HfNbTiVAl10.
generation.boundary: This approach may fail when the microstructural features are not adequately characterized or when extreme local heterogeneities (e.g., unexpected phase segregation or nano-scale defects not captured in the descriptors) dominate the mechanical response.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal selection and quantification of the microstructural descriptors and how well they generalize across different processing conditions, as well as potential nonlinear effects at varying strain rates.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of standardized tensile and fracture tests on multiple as‐cast HfNbTiVAl10 specimens at room temperature (strain rate ≈ 10^(-3) s^(–1)), while concurrently characterizing their hierarchical microstructures using SEM/TEM. Use the collected microstructural data as input into the machine learning surrogate model to predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior. Compare the model predictions with the experimental measurements.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves to extract yield strength and Young’s modulus
Fracture surface analysis and nanoindentation measurements for fracture toughness
Quantitative microstructural characterization (phase fractions, lattice distortions, precipitate sizes)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured mechanical properties consistently deviate from the surrogate model predictions by more than 20% across multiple independent tests, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The tensile stress–strain curves of the NbTaTiZrV0.5 RHEA at room temperature (RT) and high temperature (673–1273 K) are presented in Figure 4a. The tensile properties of this HEA were shown to be in agreement with a previous study []. At room temperature, the cold-rolled alloy showed excellent tensile properties, with a yield strength approaching 1200 MPa and a plasticity reaching 8%. When the temperature reached 673 K, the strain–stress curve revealed a serrated flow behavior at a constant strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1, while the strength decreased, and the plasticity increased greatly. This occurred mainly in the softening phase, which may be related to the reason for the improvement in the plasticity []. When the temperature increased further, the yield strength and plasticity of the alloy decreased stably, but the decreasing range was small. The yield strength decreased significantly, and the plasticity rose to more than 30% when the temperature increased to 1223 K.

In this study, the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA were tested at elevated temperatures. Additionally, XRD, SEM, and TEM were used to thoroughly characterize the samples both before and after testing. The results are summarized below: Over a wide temperature range of RT-1223 K, the studied alloy exhibited excellent tensile mechanical properties. From RT to 678 K, the strength of the alloy was maintained above 1000 MPa; At 878–1078 K, the strength variation was small and no less than 800 MPa, and it nearly exceeded most commercial alloys. Coupled with an excellent cold workability, the alloy has the potential to be used as a new generation of high-temperature materials for the preparation of high-temperature-resistant parts in aerospace. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions showed similar trends at temperatures between 873 K and 1073 K. That is, a work hardening occurred after yielding, and then a gradual softening until fracture. cited_evidence.text: We optimized the RFR model by tuning key hyperparameters through a grid search, ensuring robust and accurate predictions. To assess the generalizability of our RFR model, we employed 10-fold cross-validation (10 CV). This method splits the data into 10-folds, using 9-folds for training and 1-fold for testing, and repeats the process 10 times with each fold serving as the test set once. This comprehensive evaluation ensures the robustness and generalizability of the model’s performance. Using 10 CV, the RFR model achieved a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 9.19% for plasticity εf and 182.28 MPa for yield strength σYS. Plots comparing the measured and predicted values, shown in Figure 3, revealed a high R² value of 0.86 for yield strength, indicating a clear linear trend. In contrast, the R² value for plasticity was lower, at 0.66, reflecting greater data dispersion. This discrepancy likely stems from plasticity’s higher sensitivity to microstructural variations introduced during casting and processing, such as grain size and phase distribution, which are less consistent across different studies []. The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. Fracture toughness (KIC) represents the ability of a material to prevent crack propagation, similar to hardness and Young's modulus, and it is highly related to the bond energy of component oxides and the density of obtained glass samples. As presented in Figure 5B, the fracture toughness of the high-entropy glasses increases with R changing from La to Gd. This can be partly owing to the increased glass density from R = La to Gd (Figures 6A and 6B). On the other hand, a decrease in the ionic radii of R increases the bond energy, and more energies are needed to crack extending, which result in the enhancement of fracture toughness. As presented in Figure 5C, the prepared high-entropy glasses exhibit extraordinary fracture toughness compared with the commercial oxide glasses (borates, silicates, borosilicates, etc. [; ; ; ; ; ; ; ]) and the current high fracture toughness oxide glasses (; ).
